report.source_text: The patient's chronic axial mechanical neck pain and bilateral upper extremity radiculopathy correlated with the degenerative and stenotic segments from C3 through C7. The pruritus was possibly caused by compression of the nerve roots and/or spinal cord at the affected levels. Given his multiyear history of multimodal conservative therapies and correlation between imaging and physical examination, it was thought that surgical intervention in the form of an ACDF from C3 to C7 would provide the patient permanent relief of his pain and pruritus.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old male nurse practitioner presented with a 6-year history of disabling bilateral upper extremity pruritus in the C6 dermatomal distribution, concurrent with bilateral neck pain, limited cervical range of motion, and symptoms exacerbated by neck reaching and lateral rotation. Extensive prior evaluation by dermatology, rheumatology, neurology, and psychiatry ruled out primary dermatologic disease and peripheral neuropathy. Physical examination revealed positive bilateral Spurling signs (indicating cervical radiculopathy), grossly normal skin, normal strength (5/5), symmetric reflexes (2+), and no decreased sensation. Imaging studies (spinal radiographs and cervical MRI) demonstrated multilevel cervical spondylosis with spinal stenosis at C3-4 and C4-5 with early cord flattening, and multilevel foraminal stenosis from C3 to C7. Multiple epidural steroid injections provided only transient symptom relief. Clinical assessment attributed the pruritus to nerve root and/or spinal cord compression at the affected cervical levels. The patient underwent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) from C3 to C7 without complication. Postoperatively, the patient experienced immediate symptom improvement, with 95% improvement in preoperative symptoms at 4 months follow-up and only occasional pruritus sensation. BRP is identified as a unique neuropathic condition that spine surgeons should be aware of.

final.final_diagnosis: Brachioradial Pruritus (BRP) secondary to cervical radiculopathy from multilevel cervical spondylosis
final.trajectory_summary: A 56-year-old male nurse practitioner presented with a 6-year history of disabling bilateral upper extremity pruritus in the C6 dermatomal distribution, concurrent with bilateral neck pain, limited cervical range of motion, and symptoms exacerbated by neck reaching and lateral rotation. Extensive prior evaluation by dermatology, rheumatology, neurology, and psychiatry ruled out primary dermatologic disease and peripheral neuropathy. Physical examination revealed positive bilateral Spurling signs (indicating cervical radiculopathy), grossly normal skin, normal strength (5/5), symmetric reflexes (2+), and no decreased sensation. Imaging studies (spinal radiographs and cervical MRI) demonstrated multilevel cervical spondylosis with spinal stenosis at C3-4 and C4-5 with early cord flattening, and multilevel foraminal stenosis from C3 to C7. Multiple epidural steroid injections provided only transient symptom relief. Clinical assessment attributed the pruritus to nerve root and/or spinal cord compression at the affected cervical levels. The patient underwent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) from C3 to C7 without complication. Postoperatively, the patient experienced immediate symptom improvement, with 95% improvement in preoperative symptoms at 4 months follow-up and only occasional pruritus sensation. BRP is identified as a unique neuropathic condition that spine surgeons should be aware of.
